\section[el imprevisto]{el imprevisto — the unexpected problem; unforeseen}

\label{lesson:ES-C616-imprevisto}



\begin{quote}
Before the new one: say the Spanish for the intention, then the Spanish for to set out to.
\end{quote}

\subsection*{You'll want to know: el imprevisto}
\textbf{el imprevisto} — \textquotedblleft{}the unexpected problem; unforeseen\textquotedblright{}.

\begin{quote}
Tuve un imprevisto y llegué tarde.
\end{quote}

\begin{quote}
\emph{Something came up and I arrived late.}
\end{quote}

\emph{Tener un imprevisto} — something unexpected comes up.

\begin{cousinweb}
\emph{imprevisto} is built on \emph{previsto}, the participle of \emph{prever}, a learned borrowing from Latin \emph{praevidere} 'to foresee', with \emph{in-} 'not' (EtymDB).
\end{cousinweb}

\begin{grammarlens}[title={What you've built}]
One more word for telling, explaining and describing at B1.
\end{grammarlens}

\subsection*{Your turn}
\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \emph{Say it:} \emph{el imprevisto}
  \item \emph{Say it:} \emph{el imprevisto}, once more
  \item \emph{Say it:} a sentence of your own with \emph{el imprevisto}
  \item \emph{Recall:} say the Spanish for the intention, then the Spanish for to set out to, then say \emph{el imprevisto} again
\end{itemize}

\begin{tcolorbox}[breakable,colback=teal!4,colframe=teal!35!black,title={Before you move on}]
What does el imprevisto mean? (\textquotedblleft{}The unexpected problem; unforeseen\textquotedblright{}.) Say it once more.
\end{tcolorbox}
\section[anticipar]{anticipar — to bring forward; to anticipate}

\label{lesson:ES-C616-anticipar}



\begin{quote}
Before the new one: say the Spanish for to set out to, then the Spanish for the unexpected problem.
\end{quote}

\subsection*{You'll want to know: anticipar}
\textbf{anticipar} — \textquotedblleft{}to bring forward; to anticipate\textquotedblright{}.

\begin{quote}
Anticipamos la reunión al viernes.
\end{quote}

\begin{quote}
\emph{We brought the meeting forward to Friday.}
\end{quote}

\emph{Adelantar} is more everyday. \emph{Anticiparse a} — to get ahead of.

\begin{cousinweb}
\emph{anticipar} is a learned borrowing from Latin \emph{anticipare} 'to take beforehand', built from \emph{ante} and \emph{capere} 'to take' (EtymDB).
\end{cousinweb}

\begin{grammarlens}[title={What you've built}]
One more word for telling, explaining and describing at B1.
\end{grammarlens}

\subsection*{Your turn}
\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \emph{Say it:} \emph{anticipar}
  \item \emph{Say it:} \emph{anticipar}, once more
  \item \emph{Say it:} a sentence of your own with \emph{anticipar}
  \item \emph{Recall:} say the Spanish for to set out to, then the Spanish for the unexpected problem, then say \emph{anticipar} again
\end{itemize}

\begin{tcolorbox}[breakable,colback=teal!4,colframe=teal!35!black,title={Before you move on}]
What does anticipar mean? (\textquotedblleft{}To bring forward; to anticipate\textquotedblright{}.) Say it once more.

\section[posponer]{posponer — to postpone}

\label{lesson:ES-C616-posponer}



\begin{quote}
Before the new one: say the Spanish for the unexpected problem, then the Spanish for to bring forward.
\end{quote}

\subsection*{You'll want to know: posponer}
\textbf{posponer} — \textquotedblleft{}to postpone\textquotedblright{}.

\begin{quote}
Tuvimos que posponer el viaje.
\end{quote}

\begin{quote}
\emph{We had to postpone the trip.}
\end{quote}

Like \emph{poner}: \emph{pospongo, pospuse}.

\begin{cousinweb}
\emph{posponer} is a learned borrowing from Latin \emph{postponere} 'to put after', built from \emph{post} and \emph{ponere} 'to put' (Lewis \& Short).
\end{cousinweb}

\begin{grammarlens}[title={What you've built}]
One more word for telling, explaining and describing at B1.
\end{grammarlens}

  \item \emph{Say it:} \emph{posponer}, once more
  \item \emph{Say it:} a sentence of your own with \emph{posponer}
  \item \emph{Recall:} say the Spanish for the unexpected problem, then the Spanish for to bring forward, then say \emph{posponer} again

\section[el contratiempo]{el contratiempo — the setback, the mishap}

\label{lesson:ES-C616-contratiempo}



\begin{quote}
Before the new one: say the Spanish for to bring forward, then the Spanish for to postpone.
\end{quote}

\subsection*{You'll want to know: el contratiempo}
\textbf{el contratiempo} — \textquotedblleft{}the setback, the mishap\textquotedblright{}.

\begin{quote}
Tuvimos un contratiempo con el coche.
\end{quote}

\begin{quote}
\emph{We had a setback with the car.}
\end{quote}

A small problem that upsets a plan.

\begin{cousinweb}
\emph{contratiempo} is built from \emph{contra} 'against' and \emph{tiempo}, inherited from Latin \emph{tempus} 'time' (Lewis \& Short).
\end{cousinweb}

\begin{grammarlens}[title={What you've built}]
One more word for telling, explaining and describing at B1.
\end{grammarlens}

\section[la alternativa]{la alternativa — the alternative, the other option}

\label{lesson:ES-C616-alternativa}



\begin{quote}
Before the new one: say the Spanish for to postpone, then the Spanish for the setback.
\end{quote}

\subsection*{You'll want to know: la alternativa}
\textbf{la alternativa} — \textquotedblleft{}the alternative, the other option\textquotedblright{}.

\begin{quote}
No hay otra alternativa.
\end{quote}

\begin{quote}
\emph{There is no other alternative.}
\end{quote}

Also an adjective: \emph{una ruta alternativa}.

\begin{cousinweb}
\emph{alternativa} is built on \emph{alternar} and \emph{alterno}, learned borrowings from Latin \emph{alternare} and \emph{alternus} 'by turns', from \emph{alter} 'the other' (EtymDB).
\end{cousinweb}

\begin{grammarlens}[title={What you've built}]
One more word for telling, explaining and describing at B1.
\end{grammarlens}
